ch07 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: The editors' introduction retells two origin stories of D&D: Gygax and Arneson extending Tolkien fandom and 1970s tabletop wargames, and Gygax's childhood friend Jim Rausch staging live make-believe spy games. It asks whether D&D is a wargame, an art form, or something that resists definition, invoking Wittgenstein's claim that 'game' covers too diverse a range of activities to be defined and Huizinga's Homo Ludens on play standing outside truth and falsity, good and evil. It then frames the volume's guiding questions: whether basement role-playing is mere escapism or a proving ground for ideas, whether players invent new moralities for strange worlds, and what standard of value 'good game' invokes.

chapters.file: ch08 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
ch09 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Littmann answers the charge that D&D is a waste of time with Aristotle: pleasure is good as an end in itself, humanity's function is thinking, so even munchkin power-gaming and 4E combat roles are worthwhile intellectual activity under the function argument. He then treats D&D as participatory art—improvisational storytelling offering catharsis (smacking goblins to purge aggression) and the Poetics' license to explore what could be, like the dwarf chieftain grieving a disintegrated son or deciding what a friend owes the thief in the scorpion nest. A good DM, on this Aristotelian view, makes plots unfold with internal probability and characters act from consistent personality, yet 'just playing my character' never excuses ruining another player's fun, since artistic value never suspends the virtues governing how we treat people.

chapters.file: ch10 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Merli argues that good role-playing refutes Aristotelian virtue ethics: decent players convincingly play genuinely evil thieves and morally mediocre players play truly virtuous paladins, so the skill of judging what the virtuous agent would do cannot require being virtuous or having the habituated emotions McDowell, Hursthouse, and Jacobson say are necessary to 'see what to do'. Using a dice-guessing versus unverifiable aura-reading analogy, he shows that the virtue ethicist's escape—denying non-virtuous players can get it right—makes virtuous judgment look fraudulent and untestable. Because role-playing demands active first-person deliberation rather than the passive reception of literary fiction, it exposes that judging rightly and being virtuous are distinct skills, with implications for how habituation and moral education work.

chapters.file: ch11 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Cogburn protests Fourth Edition's contraction of the nine alignments and rebuilds the system philosophically: Lawful means willing universalizable law in Kant's categorical-imperative sense (the liar and murderer treating themselves as exceptions), Good means willing the greatest happiness in Mill's utilitarian sense, yielding a nine-box grid of moral psychologies. He populates it with fantasy archetypes—Haomane Firstborn as pathological Lawful Neutral, Karsa Orlong as Chaotic Neutral, Abercrombie's torturer Glotka as Neutral Neutral in Hannah Arendt's 'banality of evil' mold, hierarchic vampires and cynical politicians as Lawful Evil, Conan's raiders as Chaotic Evil. On this scheme Chaotic Good is genuinely empty, Drizzt and Robin Hood types are really Lawful or Neutral Good, and a Neutral Good versus Lawful Good dispute over killing one innocent to save thousands shows how gameplay can stage classic ethics thought experiments.

chapters.file: ch12 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Bateman replies to Cogburn that Law and Chaos descend not from Kant but from Michael Moorcock's Eternal Champion stories, where they are liberal and conservative political tendencies held in check by the Cosmic Balance, which restores Chaotic Good, Lawful Evil, and the Druid's true Neutral as viable positions. He rejects the 'sausage machine' universalization of maxims for Kant's humanity formula and Realm of Ends, and argues act utilitarianism makes a poor model of Good: an overpopulation scenario could mandate genocide, and Bentham's felicific calculus cannot actually measure the good. Alain Badiou's ethic of truths supplies the positive case for Chaotic Good—pursuing what you take to be good without submitting to a single moral law—while Buddhist and Jain renunciation dignifies Lawful Neutral.

chapters.file: ch13 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Silcox recalls his middle-school Paladin dying to eighty-three orcs while his friends held a memorial service, and asks whether grief for a player character is irrational. He tests Charles Taylor's narrative ethics—the thesis that we grasp our lives as unfolding stories—finding it challenged by Beckett's Godot, the novel-within-a-novel of Atonement, and Samantha Vice's warnings about story-shaped lives, and he notes leveling up and 4E's heroic PCs make characters story-like in ways ordinary lives are not. Ultimately PC death differs from real death because the campaign's story continues without the character, whereas death, as Nagel argues, cuts off our open-ended future; Silcox ends by recasting the self as a 'back-story' or metanarrative that enables storytelling, rejecting Descartes' claim that the power of imagination is inessential to our essence.

chapters.file: ch14 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Dadlez recounts playing an evil Romulan spy who befriended the Enterprise crew, blew up the ship, and got shunned by her real friends, and asks whether role-playing villains makes players complicit in immoral perspectives. Working from Hume on fiction that describes 'vicious manners' without disapprobation, and the imaginative-resistance debate (Walton, Gendler), she argues the role-player is like an author or improvisational actor who makes it fictional that a character holds wicked views without imaginatively endorsing them—no utilitarian or deontological truth of the game world endorsed her sabotage. Her friends' anger was really at her hijacking a collaborative story into one where the villain wins, and her only residual worry about the 'Orc Holocaust' of experience-point slaughter is that game generalizations about inherently hostile monsters might bleed into real-world prejudice about human groups.

chapters.file: ch15 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Cooke defends his three-year lawful-evil wizard campaign against religious and secular critics by dismantling each style of argument. The propaganda charge fails because D&D rulebooks present no 'attitudes for export' about the real world; the puzzle of imaginative resistance dissolves once Can'tian and Won'tian readings are rejected for a 'Hardian' view that some things are merely hard to imagine, undercutting Dadlez's explanation of the Romulan spy's angry opponents; and the Werther-effect-style empirical case against D&D collapses on the data like parallel panics over jazz, video games, and pornography. The remaining character-warping objection—the Platonic and Aristotelian habituation worry that enjoying evil play mistrains the sentiments Hume warned about—turns unfalsifiable in the way repressed-desire claims do, leaving a firm moral gap between imagining evil and doing it.

chapters.file: ch16 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: The Rochas confess to being 'elf racists' about drow and use D&D's elf subspecies to stage the philosophy of race: since human races are not biologically real (no race gene, and greater genomic diversity within Africa than between continents), the Forgotten Realms' elf races work only as stereotypes—wood elves as nature-loving Native Americans, sun elves as model-minority Asians, moon elves as the unmarked white norm, and drow as the inherently evil dark-skinned race whose Underdark mirrors the American ghetto, with redeemed dark elves echoing the racist 'good negro' of lighter skin. Weighing W.E.B. Du Bois's conservation-of-races hope that each group prove its unique message, and Lucius Outlaw's view of race as a support group, against Kwame Anthony Appiah's warning that keeping races inevitably regenerates racism, they conclude racial thinking always slides into hierarchy. The remedy is anti-lazy DMing: build worlds with species differences but individuals who can surprise.

chapters.file: ch17 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Olson opens with her own first session, in which the DM steered her toward a 'sexy Eladrin' miniature in high heels, and asks why women stay away from D&D. She argues the game's mechanics are egalitarian—identical power lists for male and female characters, echoing Plato's Republic claim that women guard the city by the same nature as men—and that party cooperation embodies the relational, care-based feminist ethic Marilyn Friedman and Angela Bolte oppose to male-coded individualism. The trouble is culture, not system: sexualized miniatures that objectify female bodies, tokenism, harassment, and marketing that ignores women, to which female gamers respond by playing male characters like Jenni Dowsett, designing separatist systems such as Portal Worlds, or, like Shelly Mazzanoble, claiming D&D for the 'inner girl'.

chapters.file: ch18 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
ch19 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Silcox and Cox present D&D modules as thought experiments in James Robert Brown's 'laboratory of the mind': the Tomb of Horrors' plane-shifting doorway forces Parfit's teletransporter question of whether the character who emerges is you, a copy, or an annihilation, extended to Tieflings and Warforged; Eberron's sentient Warforged raise Nagel's bat problem of whether a human player can know what it is like to be a machine, answered with the conclusion that players really explore human pretense, like Greek actors in masks. Mary Anne Warren's Space Traveler criteria for alien personhood strain against orcs who meet them yet attack on sight, and against the players who killed the lawful-good Flumph without parley. The deep difference is perspective: philosophy imagines sub specie aeternitatis while D&D demands immersion sub specie temporis, which nonetheless cultivates the open-minded intellectual virtues philosophers prize.

chapters.file: ch20 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Cogburn and Hebert sort fantasy magic into formulaic natural magic (wizards as scientists exploiting a world's universal laws, in Kant's sense of nature—Salvatore's Cadderly, Snape's potions, Eberron's Artificer), sublimate natural magic (shamans, sorcerers, and warlocks surrendering to forces, as in African diaspora possession religions), and unnatural magic that violates a world's laws, whose horror Sartre's Nausea passage about flesh rebelling captures. Using Lovecraft's indescribable monsters and Noël Carroll's theory of art-horror as categorical impurity (with Mary Douglas on Leviticus-style purity codes), they argue Fourth Edition's algorithmic spell rules make casting feel like chemistry homework rather than the impossible, so unnatural magic cannot be modeled ludologically. Dungeon Masters must instead express the inexpressible through narrative techniques—character reaction, reader-relative impossibility, and limit impossibility—since D&D at its best is shared storytelling, not rule fetishism.

chapters.file: ch21 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Morton reads D&D as a hands-on workshop in phenomenology: mapping dungeons and caring for fellow party members enact Heideggerian 'worlding', while module texts like the blood-stained, smudged journal in The Lost Caverns of Tsojcanth—alluding to Moria's dwarf-record—show that worlds are opaque, alluring, and never transparent. Developing Graham Harman's 'sincerity' (you cannot jump outside your phenomenological skin) and 'allure', he argues each character class and alignment plane constitutes its own untotalizable world, with the Illusionist a recursive figure for a game already built on illusion, and he situates D&D at the end of realism's history of narrative control, mixing Wagnerian Gesamtkunstwerk with constructivist demystification. What happens in melee rounds is not Coleridge's willing suspension of disbelief but its opposite, a 'willing disbelief' that punctures Romantic immersion to get on with earning experience points.

holes.name: Catharsis (Poetics on tragedy and fiction)
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Poetics that tragedy purges pity and fear and that poetry, depicting what might be, is more philosophical than history.
holes.why: Chapter 9's central defense of D&D as worthwhile art runs through catharsis and the Poetics, which the taxonomy's other Aristotle slugs (eudaimonia, virtue ethics) do not cover.

holes.name: Alain Badiou
holes.what: Contemporary French philosopher whose 'ethic of truths' holds that enforcing a single moral law or named Good generates evil as 'simulacrum' or 'disaster'.
holes.why: Chapter 12 relies on Badiou's ethic of truths for its main conclusion that Chaotic Good is a coherent position—pursuing good without accepting one universal moral law.

holes.name: Charles Taylor
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of narrative identity who holds that making sense of ourselves requires grasping our lives as unfolding stories oriented to the good.
holes.why: Chapter 13 takes Taylor's narrative ethics as its main interlocutor, testing it against D&D players' grief for dead characters before revising it into a 'back-story' view of the self.

holes.name: Imaginative Resistance
holes.what: The puzzle, rooted in Hume's Standard of Taste and developed by Walton and Gendler, that readers balk at imagining moral claims they believe false even inside fantastical fiction.
holes.why: Chapter 14 explains real-world anger at evil role-play via imaginative resistance, and Chapter 15 builds its defense of evil characters on dissolving that puzzle—no taxonomy slug covers it.

holes.name: Mary Anne Warren
holes.what: Philosopher whose Space Traveler thought experiment asks how we could tell whether alien beings are persons with full moral rights (famous also for her abortion-era personhood criteria).
holes.why: Chapter 19 applies Warren's personhood criteria to orcs and the wrongly killed lawful-good Flumph to question when killing monsters is justified.

holes.name: Art-Horror (Carroll's philosophy of horror)
holes.what: Noël Carroll's theory that horror fiction expresses the indescribable through monsters that are categorically impure, incomplete, or formless relative to the audience's conceptual scheme.
holes.why: Chapter 20 builds its entire account of why D&D's rule-based magic cannot model Lovecraftian unnatural magic on Carroll's art-horror apparatus, none of which the taxonomy captures.

holes.name: Graham Harman
holes.what: Philosopher of Object-Oriented Ontology, holding that real objects are radically unknowable and that aesthetic 'allure' discloses their hidden reality.
holes.why: Chapter 21 develops its account of D&D worlds and character-class 'sincerities' directly from Harman's concepts of allure and sincerity.
